title: Explain OOP through all seven concepts (abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, composition, aggregation, association), and why OOP is important (modularity, maintainability, real-world modeling).
shortTitle: What are all seven OOP concepts?

s1_definition.profdef: Beyond the four pillars (encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism), OOP includes three RELATIONSHIP concepts that describe how objects collaborate. ASSOCIATION is the most general — "object A USES object B" (any relationship: TradeService uses TradeRepository). AGGREGATION is a WEAK HAS-A relationship — "object A HAS object B, but B can exist independently" (Department HAS Employees, but Employees exist even if Department is dissolved). COMPOSITION is a STRONG HAS-A relationship — "object A OWNS object B, and B cannot exist without A" (Account OWNS Transactions — if the Account is deleted, its Transactions are meaningless and also deleted). Together, all seven concepts enable OOP's three core benefits: MODULARITY (each class is a self-contained unit), MAINTAINABILITY (change one class without breaking others), and REAL-WORLD MODELING (bank accounts, trades, customers map naturally to objects).
s1_definition.analogy: ASSOCIATION: the bank's TradeService USES the MarketDataProvider — they know each other but neither owns the other. If the market data provider changes to a different vendor, the trade service switches but both continue to exist independently.
s1_definition.oneliner: 4 pillars: encapsulate, abstract, inherit, polymorph. 3 relationships: association (uses), aggregation (has-A, weak), composition (owns-A, strong — lifecycle bound). Together: modularity + maintainability + real-world modeling.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Beyond the four pillars (encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism), OOP includes three RELATIONSHIP concepts that describe how objects collaborate. ASSOCIATION is the most general — "object A USES object B" (any relationship: TradeService uses TradeRepository). AGGREGATION is a WEAK HAS-A relationship — "object A HAS object B, but B can exist independently" (Department HAS Employees, but Employees exist even if Department is dissolved). COMPOSITION is a STRONG HAS-A relationship — "object A OWNS object B, and B cannot exist without A" (Account OWNS Transactions — if the Account is deleted, its Transactions are meaningless and also deleted). Together, all seven concepts enable OOP's three core benefits: MODULARITY (each class is a self-contained unit), MAINTAINABILITY (change one class without breaking others), and REAL-WORLD MODELING (bank accounts, trades, customers map naturally to objects).

**In simple words (banking analogy):**

ASSOCIATION: the bank's TradeService USES the MarketDataProvider — they know each other but neither owns the other. If the market data provider changes to a different vendor, the trade service switches but both continue to exist independently.

AGGREGATION: the Trading DEPARTMENT has a list of Traders. If the department is reorganized, the traders still exist — they move to another department. Traders are NOT destroyed when the department changes. Weak ownership.

COMPOSITION: Rajesh's Account has Transactions (deposit, withdrawal records). If Rajesh's Account is CLOSED (deleted), ALL its transactions are also deleted — they have no meaning without the account. Strong ownership. In JPA: `cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true`.

**One line to remember:** 4 pillars: encapsulate, abstract, inherit, polymorph. 3 relationships: association (uses), aggregation (has-A, weak), composition (owns-A, strong — lifecycle bound). Together: modularity + maintainability + real-world modeling.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's trading system needs to model real-world relationships.** A TradingDepartment HAS traders (aggregation — traders exist independently). Each Trade OWNS its list of Fees (composition — fees are meaningless without the trade). The SettlementService USES the ClearingHouse (association — independent services). The developer initially used inheritance for everything (Trade extends Fee?!) — wrong. The team refactors to use the correct relationship type for each: association for service-to-service collaboration, aggregation for department-to-trader (weak ownership), and composition for trade-to-fees (strong ownership, cascade delete).

**What the project will show:** All three relationship types in one system, association (SettlementService uses ClearingHouse), aggregation (TradingDepartment has Traders), composition (Trade owns Fees with cascade delete), JPA mapping for each (@ManyToOne, @OneToMany with/without cascade), and the three benefits (modularity, maintainability, real-world modeling).

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 — ASSOCIATION.** SettlementService has a reference to ClearingHouse (injected by Spring). SettlementService calls `clearingHouse.clearTrade("TRD-001")`. Both services exist independently — replacing ClearingHouse with a different vendor requires ZERO changes to SettlementService.

**Step 2 — AGGREGATION.** Trader Rajesh and Trader Priya are created independently. They are ADDED to the Equity Trading Desk (aggregation). The desk is DISSOLVED — `dissolve()` removes traders from the list and returns them. Rajesh and Priya SURVIVE — they are added to the new Global Trading Desk. Traders existed BEFORE the department and exist AFTER it.

**Step 3 — COMPOSITION.** Trade TRD-001 is created for RELIANCE Rs.245,050. The Trade's constructor CREATES three Fee objects (BROKERAGE, GST, STT). These fees are OWNED by the trade — they were created BY the trade, stored inside the trade, and returned as an unmodifiable view. If the trade is deleted, the fees are garbage collected (no external reference to them).

**Step 4 — The KEY difference.** Department dissolved → Rajesh survives (AGGREGATION: weak ownership). Trade deleted → BROKERAGE fee destroyed (COMPOSITION: strong ownership, lifecycle bound).

**Step 5 — Why OOP matters.** Modularity: Trade class handles trade logic + fee calculation. TradingDepartment handles department roster. Neither knows about the other. Maintainability: changing fee calculation (add new fee type) requires changing ONLY Trade.java. Departmention, SettlementService, ClearingHouse — all unchanged. Real-world modeling: trades, fees, traders, departments — the code structure mirrors the banking domain.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ THREE RELATIONSHIP TYPES ═══

  ASSOCIATION (uses — weakest coupling):
    SettlementService ——→ ClearingHouse
    "I use you, but I don't own you"
    Both exist independently. Spring injection.
    In UML: plain arrow ——→

  AGGREGATION (has-A — weak ownership):
    TradingDepartment ◇——→ Trader
    "I have traders, but they survive without me"
    Department dissolved → traders live on
    In UML: hollow diamond ◇——→
    In JPA: @OneToMany WITHOUT cascade delete

  COMPOSITION (owns-A — strong ownership):
    Trade ◆——→ Fee
    "I own fees. They die with me."
    Trade deleted → fees deleted
    In UML: filled diamond ◆——→
    In JPA: @OneToMany(cascade=ALL, orphanRemoval=true)

  ═══ LIFECYCLE COMPARISON ═══

  Create parent  → Association: target exists independently
                  → Aggregation: children exist independently (added later)
                  → Composition: children CREATED by parent

  Delete parent  → Association: target unaffected
                  → Aggregation: children SURVIVE
                  → Composition: children DESTROYED

  ═══ WHY OOP MATTERS ═══

  MODULARITY: each class is self-contained (Trade, Fee, Trader, Department)
  MAINTAINABILITY: change one class → others unchanged
  REAL-WORLD MODELING: objects = real banking entities
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
OOP has seven concepts: four pillars (encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism) and three relationship types (association, aggregation, composition). Association is the weakest — object A uses object B, both exist independently (SettlementService uses ClearingHouse). Aggregation is weak HAS-A — parent contains children but children survive if the parent is destroyed (TradingDepartment has Traders — traders move to another department when the desk is dissolved). Composition is strong HAS-A — parent OWNS children, children are created by the parent and destroyed with it (Trade owns Fees — deleting a trade deletes all its fees).

In my trading relationships service, the three types coexist in one system. SettlementService is ASSOCIATED with ClearingHouse through Spring dependency injection — replace the clearing house implementation and the settlement service continues unchanged. TradingDepartment AGGREGATES Traders — dissolving the department returns the traders who can join a new department. Trade COMPOSES Fees — the constructor creates three fees (brokerage, GST, STT) that are permanently bound to the trade, returned as an unmodifiable view, and garbage collected when the trade is deleted. In JPA, composition maps to `cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true` — aggregation does NOT cascade deletes.

OOP matters because of three benefits: MODULARITY — each class is a self-contained unit that can be developed and tested independently. MAINTAINABILITY — changing fee calculation logic in Trade.java requires zero changes to TradingDepartment, SettlementService, or ClearingHouse. REAL-WORLD MODELING — the code structure mirrors the banking domain: trades have fees, departments have traders, services use other services — exactly how the real bank operates.
